world_behind.title: Isaiah, opened up
world_behind.text: Most of this chapter runs along Isaiah 29, but the middle of it is not in Isaiah at all. Verses 6 through 23 expand a two-verse figure about a sealed book into a detailed account of how a record is delivered, withheld, shown to witnesses, and read. Nephi is not quoting here so much as unfolding.

world_behind.title: What "sealed" meant
world_behind.text: Ancient documents were closed with clay or wax and a signet, and a sealed document could be carried, stored, and inherited without being read. Isaiah's figure assumes that everyday object. The chapter then presses it further than the figure usually goes: part of the book stays sealed after the rest is delivered.

world_behind.title: Housetops
world_behind.text: Verse 11 promises the sealed words read "upon the house tops" (v. 11). Flat roofs were where announcements were made in a Near Eastern town, the closest thing a village had to broadcast. The figure is not about height but about publicity, and it is the exact opposite of a sealed document.

world_behind.title: Three, and then more
world_behind.text: Verse 12 promises three witnesses and verse 13 adds "a few according to the will of God" (v. 13). The number matches the legal standard Nephi cited in chapter 11 for establishing a matter, and the record's own last books return to it when they describe the same event.

cites.quote: a few according to the will of God

spans.text: a few according to the will of God

world_behind.title: Deep sleep, and covered seers
world_behind.text: Verse 5 describes a people whose eyes are closed and whose seers are covered, which in Isaiah is the condition that makes the book necessary. The chapter's remedy is not better prophets but a book, and its recipients are explicitly the deaf and the blind of verse 29.

world_behind.title: Written to people not yet born
world_behind.text: The audience shifts in verse 1 to the last days and never comes back. Nephi's colony would not see any of this. The chapter is the clearest case in the record of a writer addressing readers he will never meet, and it describes the object those readers are holding.

words.text: Dimness, the state of being hard to make out, rather than the modern sense of being unknown. Paired with darkness, it describes what the blind see out of once the book arrives. The verse promises not brightness but resolution: things become legible.

One who mocks, a settled type in the wisdom books rather than an occasional mood. He appears in a list with the terrible one and those who watch for iniquity, and all three are described as consumed or cut off. What ends is a role, not a person's temper.

The color of fear or shame in a face. Jacob will not now wax pale, which is a promise about how a man looks rather than about what happens to him. After thirty-two verses of books, seals, and witnesses, the chapter measures the outcome by a change in countenance.

The record's oldest complaint word, attached to Laman and Lemuel from the second chapter of 1 Nephi and treated fully there. Its reappearance in the chapter's last line is the point: those who murmured shall learn doctrine. The book's effect is described on the class of people the record has been most exasperated with.

phrases.term: the words of them which have slumbered
phrases.text: The book is defined by its authors' condition before anything is said about its contents. To slumber here is to be dead, so the sleep is the grave and the waking is publication; it is the gentler version of the figure Nephi used one chapter earlier about a voice out of the ground. Dead writers, and a reader in a distant age: a strange way to introduce scripture and a natural way to introduce this particular record.

Stated flatly, and then complicated for fourteen verses: sealed, kept from the wicked, delivered to a man, partly delivered to another, partly withheld, and eventually read from the housetops. Isaiah's two verses about a sealed book become a procedure with stages, and the sealing is what makes the stages necessary.

The number is not chosen at random. Nephi had argued in chapter 11 that "by the words of three, God hath said, I will establish my word" (2 Ne. 11:3), citing the courtroom rule. Here the rule is applied to an object rather than to a doctrine, and the record's later writers describe the same arrangement when their turn comes.

phrases.term: as many witnesses as seemeth him good
phrases.text: Immediately after fixing the number at three, the chapter loosens it again, exactly as chapter 11 did after citing the legal minimum. Both passages set a floor and then say God is not bound by it. The pattern is consistent enough across the record to be a settled position rather than a hedge.

The learned man's line, and the scene's hinge. He has asked for the book, been given words instead, and answers that the sealed part cannot be read. Nothing in the exchange is hostile. The learned man is simply, accurately, unable, and the chapter treats that as the whole point rather than as an insult.

phrases.term: I am able to do mine own work
phrases.text: Said twice within two verses, which is the chapter's way of underlining. It answers the learned man's inability and the unlearned man's protest at once, and it is the reason given for both the sealing and the eventual unsealing. The sentence is about method as much as about power.

phrases.term: the same yesterday, today, and forever
phrases.text: The constancy formula, first sounded in this record at 1 Nephi 10:18 and treated there. Here it is God's own self-description, offered as the ground for working miracles in a late age. What the earlier passage stated as doctrine is used here as an argument: if he is unchanged, then this is not too late.

The qualification attached to the miracles in the same breath as the constancy. God is the same, and he works among people according to what they bring. Read with the sentence before it, the verse locates the variable on the human side without making the divine side conditional, which is a distinction the record keeps making.

phrases.term: draw near unto me with their mouth
phrases.text: Isaiah's indictment, "this people draw near me with their mouth, and with their lips do honour me" (Isa. 29:13), quoted here and quoted again by Christ against the Pharisees. Three uses of one sentence across three settings, and the complaint each time is the same distance between speech and heart, with fear taught by the precepts of men.

phrases.term: a marvelous work and a wonder
phrases.text: Nephi had already used the phrase in his own voice two chapters earlier when describing what happens when God sets his hand the second time. Here it arrives in its Isaiah setting, immediately after the indictment it answers. The record's favorite description of its own coming forth is a response to lip service.

phrases.term: Who seeth us, and who knoweth us?
phrases.text: The question of people whose works are in the dark, and it is asked in the same chapter that describes a book brought out of the ground into daylight. The chapter's whole architecture answers it: things hidden are the ones that get read from the housetops.

verses.label: v. 1–5
verses.title: A people asleep
verses.text: Nations fighting Zion become a dream of a hungry man who wakes still empty. Then the diagnosis: a spirit of deep sleep poured out, eyes closed, prophets rejected, seers covered. The chapter establishes that the ordinary channel is blocked before it introduces the extraordinary one.

verses.label: v. 6–11
verses.title: A book, and what is in it
verses.text: Words of the dead, a seal, a revelation covering the world from beginning to end, kept back in a day of wickedness. Then the promise that the sealed part will one day be read aloud from the housetops, with nothing left hidden. The chapter gives the whole arc before narrating any of it.

verses.label: v. 12–14
verses.title: Who gets to see
verses.text: Three witnesses, then a few more, then as many as God likes. The purpose stated is testimony rather than verification, and the closing line makes rejecting the word the only listed offense. For a record that will be received on other people's say-so, this is the passage that sets the terms.

verses.label: v. 15–20
verses.title: Five speeches, no heat
verses.text: A short play in five speeches. Give the words to the learned; the learned asks for the book; the man cannot bring it; the learned cannot read it; the unlearned protests his own unlearnedness and is told to read anyway. The exchange is conducted without heat, and the resolution is a sentence about God doing his own work.

verses.label: v. 21–23
verses.title: Sealed again, and the reason
verses.text: The instruction is to read, obtain witnesses, then seal the book up and hide it again. Preservation is the stated purpose, and the theology behind it is given in verse 23: a God of miracles, unchanged, working according to faith. The chapter's practical instructions and its doctrine sit in adjacent verses.

verses.label: v. 25–28
verses.title: Lips near, hearts far
verses.text: Isaiah's indictment arrives after the book material rather than before it, so the marvelous work reads as a response to a specific failure. Then the wo on those who hide counsel in the dark, and the promise that Lebanon will become a fruitful field, which is the chapter's one purely agricultural image.

verses.label: v. 29–35
verses.title: Who benefits
verses.text: Deaf hearing a book, blind eyes seeing out of dimness, the meek increasing, the poor rejoicing, the scorner consumed, and finally those who erred coming to understanding and those who murmured learning doctrine. Every beneficiary named is someone who lacked something, and the last two named are people who had been getting it wrong.

chapter.title: Isaiah expanded rather than quoted
chapter.text: The chapter follows Isaiah 29 at both ends and departs from it entirely in the middle. Nephi had promised plainness after the block; this is what plainness looks like applied to a prophecy, and it is the most extensive expansion of a biblical passage in the record so far.

chapter.title: A book replaces a prophet
chapter.text: The people described have closed their eyes and had their seers covered. What God sends is not another seer but a volume, delivered through an unlearned man and attested by witnesses. The chapter is unusually specific about this substitution, and it is the record's account of why it exists in written form.

chapter.title: The witnesses are for others, not for proof
chapter.text: Verse 13 states the purpose: to bear testimony of his word unto the children of men. Nothing in the passage suggests the witnesses are there to satisfy the sceptical. They are there so that later readers have more than one mouth to hear it from, which is the same argument chapter 11 made about Isaiah, Jacob, and Nephi himself.

chapter.title: Inability is not condemned
chapter.text: The learned man says he cannot read a sealed book, and he is right. The chapter's complaint against the learned is stated separately, in verse 16, and it concerns motive: glory and gain rather than the glory of God. The distinction is easy to lose and the text keeps it.

chapter.title: The sealed portion is left sealed
chapter.text: Most of the chapter is about what will be delivered, and one strand is about what will not. The record as its readers have it is the unsealed part, and this chapter is the reason they know that. Very few books tell their readers how much of themselves is missing.

chapter.title: The last verse is the record's own hope
chapter.text: Those who murmured shall learn doctrine. The volume began with murmuring brothers and has been arguing with murmurers ever since. Ending a chapter about the book's coming forth on that sentence says what Nephi thinks the book is for.

applications.title: Check the channel before blaming the silence
applications.text: The people in this chapter have closed their own eyes. Before concluding that heaven has gone quiet, audit what you have stopped reading, stopped attending, or stopped asking.

applications.title: Read something written by the dead
applications.text: The chapter defines scripture as words of those who slumbered. Pick a passage and read it consciously as a message from someone who wrote knowing they would be gone. It changes the register of the reading.

applications.title: Let the sealed part stay sealed
applications.text: Some of what you want to know is deliberately withheld for now. Identify one question you keep circling that you have no way to answer, and set it down explicitly rather than continuing to worry it.

applications.title: Name the limitation, then move
applications.text: The unlearned man states his limitation and is told to read anyway. Name the thing you feel unqualified for, out loud, and then do the next required step without waiting to feel qualified.

applications.title: Test the lips-and-heart gap
applications.text: Take one thing you say regularly in worship and ask whether your heart is at the same distance as your mouth. The verse's diagnosis is not hypocrisy but drift, and drift is measured rather than confessed.

applications.title: Ask who taught you your fear
applications.text: The indictment ends with fear toward God taught by the precepts of men. Identify one thing you believe God expects, and trace where you actually learned it.

applications.title: Expect the murmurers to learn
applications.text: Think of the person you have written off as unteachable, possibly yourself. The chapter's last promise is aimed exactly there, and it does not require them to have been right first.

questions.text: What have I closed my eyes to that I would rather call God's silence?
Whose testimony did I actually receive this from, and have I ever thanked them?
Where am I the learned man in this scene, unable to read the thing I asked for?
What am I trying to do for God that he has said he is able to do himself?
Am I asking for miracles from a God I secretly think has changed?
What in my life is done in the dark on the assumption that nobody sees?
What doctrine might I learn if I stopped murmuring about the thing I murmur about most?
